core_obligations: Compute the derived limit termwise (proof lines 5078-5088): choose a K-injective representative with injective terms, view it as an inverse system of complexes and identify the derived limit with the termwise inverse limit.

Show the transition maps are surjective (proof lines 5091-5098): the structure morphisms of the product site are monomorphisms, so the corresponding restriction maps of an injective sheaf are surjective and the transition maps of the system of presheaves are surjective.

Identify the derived limit with the homotopy limit (proof lines 5101-5122): the pullback functors have exact left adjoints, so the truncations of the representative are K-injective, and the resulting short exact sequence of complexes of presheaves is also short exact as complexes of sheaves, whose middle and right terms compute the products in the derived category; this exhibits the derived limit as the homotopy limit of the system.
proof_roadmap: Choose a K-injective representative with injective terms and compute the derived limit as a termwise limit.
Verify that the transition maps of that system are surjective.
Use exact left adjoints and the identification of products with derived products to recognize the homotopy limit.
difficulty_reason: The lemma identifies the two notions of derived limit available for a complex on a product site: the derived functor of the limit and the homotopy limit of the inverse system of its pullbacks to the terms (statement lines 5066-5075). The proof is a complete computation: after choosing a K-injective representative with injective terms the derived limit is computed termwise (proof lines 5078-5088); surjectivity of the transition maps is deduced from the fact that the structure morphisms are monomorphisms (proof lines 5091-5098); and exactness of the left adjoints together with the identification of products with derived products exhibits the derived limit as the homotopy limit (proof lines 5101-5122). The non-formal content is the comparison of the two limit notions. The claim is H2: a computation whose inputs are named and whose steps are written out.
